video_title: Economics Professor on How to Fix The British Economy | Sir Paul Collier
gist: Oxford economist Sir Paul Collier tells Peter McCormack that Britain's ~zero per-capita growth is a threat to democracy, caused mainly by extreme centralization in the Treasury, over-financialization (domestic share of UK savings invested at home down from ~half to 4%), and powerless, broke local government. His fixes: devolve money and power to regional mayors, split the Treasury with a Ministry of Economy, rebuild local risk capital for scale-ups, tax land appreciation, cut energy costs and net-zero zeal, lower youth wages and fix NEET/benefit incentives, and rejoin a European security club.

insights.claim: Paul Collier argues no democracy has survived without per-capita growth of roughly 1-2% a year, and Britain has lacked that for a decade, calling a recent 0.1% growth print the death knell of democracy rather than cause for celebration.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Persistent UK stagnation raises political tail risk (populist swings) priced into gilts and sterling.
insights.quote: There is no example of a democracy that survived um without um reasonable uh rates of growth per capita 1 to 2% a year

insights.claim: Collier says the US has the easier problem (fast growth that only needs redistributing without killing growth), while Britain has the 'nightmare problem' of no per-capita growth at all.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Supports relative overweight of US vs UK growth exposure.
insights.quote: America's got the easier problem.

insights.claim: Collier argues the far-left and far-right 'charlatans' win by offering hope; mainstream policy needs a hopeful narrative that can survive interrogation, and the right in particular loses by offering only gloom.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Explains rising support for insurgent UK parties; frames UK political risk for markets.
insights.quote: a message of hope will always defeat a message of gloom.

insights.claim: Collier says young Britons like his 25-year-old son are voting Green because it sounds hopeful, but his son's own interest in saving to buy a home by his mid-30s against inflation is not served by Green economics.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Youth Green surge is soft and economically contingent; watch for it to fade if a credible growth message emerges.
insights.quote: My 25year-old son votes green.

insights.claim: Collier says Britain is the only major economy without a counterweight to its finance ministry; the Treasury is fixated on the annual budget, and he wants a Ministry of Economy planning 5-10 years ahead.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Splitting the Treasury would be a major UK institutional reform; watch for it in any Burnham-led government.
insights.quote: We are the only major economy which doesn't have a counterweight to the Ministry of Finance.

insights.claim: Collier claims Whitehall civil service headcount rose about 25% in the last seven to eight years while performance has tanked.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Supports a case for civil-service cuts or redeployment as a fiscal lever.
insights.quote: It's increased by 25% in the last seven or eight years.

insights.claim: In Germany around 70% of public spending runs through regional governments, versus roughly 4% in the UK; German local election turnout is 65-85% versus about 20% in Britain because local office has real power.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Quantifies how far UK devolution could go; regional spending power shifts would redirect public investment outside London.
insights.quote: Turnout in local elections is somewhere between 65 and 85%.

insights.claim: Collier relates that when Andy Burnham asked to control Manchester bus routes, the Treasury 'devolved' that power to Transport for London, so Manchester had to apply to TfL for bus funding.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Illustrates the London-centric capital allocation that a devolution agenda would reverse.
insights.quote: Andy Burnham planning bus routes in Manchester had to apply to transport for London to get his money for his bus routes.

insights.claim: Collier invokes subsidiarity, arguing many economic functions need units of 3-8 million people, the size of the Nordic and Baltic countries (e.g. Estonia) that outperform Britain.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Suggests regional combined authorities of this scale as the right level for UK growth policy.

insights.claim: Collier argues devolving to Scotland was a mistake because you should never devolve to an entity that could credibly secede; he says the SNP's roughly 70,000 members effectively set policy for about 5 million Scots, and cites Catalonia as Spain's parallel.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Implies devolution design should favour English regions/city-regions rather than nations, reducing secession risk.
insights.quote: you should never devolve to an entity which could credibly secede from the country.

insights.claim: Collier argues Brexit was fundamentally a revolt against London, which controls about 40% of UK GDP, rather than against Brussels; every English region except London voted Leave. He calls Brexit a disaster but dismisses the '8% lost growth' estimates as fantasy.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Regional inequality, not EU policy, is the underlying political risk; expect continued anti-London politics.
insights.quote: the Brexit vote was fundamentally a mutiny against London, not against Brussels.

insights.claim: Sheffield's per-capita income was far above East Germany's when German reunification began; now it is far below, which Collier blames on the Treasury, contrasting it with Helmut Kohl's cross-party 30-year solidarity tax that lifted East German productivity from one-fifth to about 80% of the West.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: A generational (25-30 year), cross-party regional investment program is his model for northern England.
insights.quote: When we when that started, Sheffield was far higher per capita income than East Germany. Now it's far lower per capita income than East Germany.

insights.claim: Collier proposes making Treasury staff redundant with preferential hiring into local government, upgrading councils such as Bedford, and argues Whitehall turns the brightest recruits into useless officials while the military turns struggling youths into productive people.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: A concrete civil-service redeployment idea that could feature in UK reform agendas.
insights.quote: White Hall takes in the most brilliant people in the country and it turns them into people who are bloody useless.

insights.claim: Peter McCormack reports Bedford council approached a Section 114 (effective bankruptcy) because statutory demands from Whitehall outpaced revenue, leaving councils across the country with no money and no powers.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: Local authority insolvency risk is widespread; relevant for local-authority lenders and municipal service providers.
insights.quote: it was approaching a section 114.

insights.claim: London-centric infrastructure spending exemplifies the problem: royal jubilees produced the Jubilee line and the Elizabeth line, national investments in London infrastructure that Collier says must be matched elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Devolution-minded governments would tilt infrastructure capex toward northern regions.

insights.claim: Collier says the share of British savings invested in Britain fell from about half 30 years ago to just 4% today, driven by specific legal-interpretation and incentive changes that can be reversed.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Policy to repatriate UK pension/insurance capital could be a major bid for UK equities, especially small and mid caps.
insights.quote: now it's down from half to just 4%.

insights.claim: Collier attributes the collapse in domestic investment to lawyers reinterpreting pension fiduciary duty from 'best efforts for a decent return' to being able to meet all obligations if liquidated any day, forcing funds into liquid, near-zero-return Treasury bills and away from risk assets.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: A reversal of this liability interpretation would shift UK pension allocations from gilts/bills toward domestic equities and growth capital.
insights.quote: So you liquidate every day. You you operate as if you had to liquidate the firm every day

insights.claim: Collier says Britain is good at start-ups thanks to strong universities but bad at scaling firms from about 4 million to 30 million and on to $100 million-$1 billion valuations, unlike the US.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: The UK scale-up gap is the investable niche: patient growth capital for £4-30m firms.
insights.quote: What we're really bad at is taking firms from a valuation of about 4 million through to valuations of 30 and then on to valuations of a billion.

insights.claim: Collier steers his son into a patient-capital investor that takes owner-managed small firms from roughly 4 million to 15 million valuations over ten years by installing boards and management systems, and says very few UK agencies do this.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Long-horizon small-company succession/growth investors fill an underserved UK niche.
insights.quote: It's exactly it's a patient capital system

insights.claim: Collier says UK private equity has a poor record of gutting firms and selling assets abroad too early, a key limitation of free markets alongside short-termism.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Political risk of tighter rules on PE takeovers of UK firms.

insights.claim: Collier argues the loss of local banks, local stock markets and local pools of public finance destroyed the tacit, local knowledge investors need, and that scale-up capital must be locally rooted, combining local public and private money.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Regional investment funds and local banks could be favored by devolution policy.
insights.quote: If you've not got local private finance, if it's all run from London, you don't know the gossip.

insights.claim: Collier cites Airbus, an alliance of about five European aircraft makers built on long-term trust and specialization, as outperforming the vertically integrated Boeing, showing capitalism succeeds through cooperation as well as competition.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Supports a structural view favoring Airbus's model and cooperative industrial clusters.
insights.quote: Airbus has outperformed Boeing, right?

insights.claim: Collier says UK energy costs are killingly high, nearly as bad as Germany's but without Germany's robust private sector to absorb them, and calls the net-zero obsession very damaging to growth.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Growing political pressure to dilute net-zero policy is a risk for UK renewables subsidies and a tailwind for energy-intensive industry.
insights.quote: the net zero thing is an obsession which is I think very damaging

insights.claim: Collier says the UK minimum wage is too high, exists only for political reasons, and wages for 18-25-year-olds should be set considerably below those of experienced workers.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Supports a policy case for lower youth wage bands; relevant for hospitality and retail labor costs.
insights.quote: I think it's only a political reason.

insights.claim: Collier says Britain has about a million young NEETs, the highest rate in Europe, incentivized onto sickness benefits that pay better than job-seeking; the Netherlands has half Britain's rate.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Welfare reform targeting youth sickness claims is likely; a fiscal and labor-supply lever.
insights.quote: it's the highest rate of needs in Europe.

insights.claim: The Dutch education model Collier recommends: students failing end-of-year tests get intensive summer remedial courses and, if still failing, repeat the year, alongside multiple vocational pathways (plumbers, welders) which Britain uniquely lacks in Europe.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Points to vocational training as a UK policy growth area.

insights.claim: McCormack says his Bedford town centre is dead due to high energy costs, regulation, business rates and minimum wages, and floats abolishing business rates locally in an economic opportunity zone even if it breaks statutory rules.
insights.speaker: Peter McCormack (host)
insights.so_what: Business rates are a key pressure on UK high-street retail economics.

insights.claim: Collier favors taxing land appreciation because Britain over-incentivizes buying property for zero-sum capital gains rather than risking money on growing businesses, which is positive-sum.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: A land-appreciation tax would be negative for UK buy-to-let and residential property valuations, positive for business investment.
insights.quote: we've all absorbed the very dangerous idea that in order to make money you just need to buy a house

insights.claim: Collier agrees large companies favour heavy regulation because they can afford compliance while smaller rivals cannot, and calls for a 'bonfire of regulation'; he says Britain's tax code is the longest in the world and raises little.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Deregulation would favour UK SMEs over incumbents.
insights.quote: we need a bonfire of regulation.

insights.claim: Collier sees corporate lobbying as a nuisance rather than a fundamental problem, citing a recent US vote where billionaire money failed to stop a shift left.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Discount the power of money to determine election outcomes.

insights.claim: Collier praises Denmark's Mette Frederiksen for telling voters welfare must be cut to fund higher military spending given the Russian threat and US retreat, rather than borrowing; his research with the IMF found Denmark had both the lowest economic hit and lowest excess mortality from COVID in Europe.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: European defence spending rising at the expense of welfare is a structural trend favouring defence contractors.
insights.quote: The best in the whole of Europe was Denmark.

insights.claim: Collier argues China is too centralized to reach the technology frontier, succeeding only in lower-end chipmaking; Xi has scared entrepreneurs, policy reversals from the one-child policy destroyed trust, and it has huge debts and a near-bankrupt construction sector.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Bearish structural view on Chinese growth and frontier tech leadership.
insights.quote: It's not at the frontiers and it never will be because it's far too centralized

insights.claim: Collier claims democratic Taiwan's per-capita income is 'something over $100,000 a year', at least double China's much lower average (his figure for China is garbled in the transcript), and attributes the gap to innovation under democracy.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Reinforces Taiwan's innovation economy as structurally superior; figures as stated are loose.
insights.quote: the little offshore place is on something over $100,000 a year that's innovation for you

insights.claim: Collier argues the US is no longer willing to defend Europe, so Britain must rejoin a European security club; he expects Europe to change fundamentally over 4-5 years toward conservatism, with Giorgia Meloni as the template and Spain's premier about to lose power.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Rightward European shift and rising defence integration; positive for European defence, relevant for EU fiscal policy.
insights.quote: why should 300 million people in America defend 500 million people in Western Europe from uh 150 million people in Russia?

insights.claim: Collier expects Marine Le Pen in power to be less fearsome than the left fears, noting she has dropped her aim of leaving Europe.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Suggests markets may over-price French populist risk.
insights.quote: I suspect Le Pen will um uh turn out to be uh not as fearsome as uh as the as the left fears.

insights.claim: Collier sees Javier Milei in Argentina as showing voters will back radical options once conditions are bad enough, and suggests Britain may need things to get worse to break its 'tyranny of complacency'.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: UK radical reform likely requires deeper crisis; near-term status quo risk.
insights.quote: the tyranny of complacency

insights.claim: Collier calls Andy Burnham the most hopeful UK politician in ten years for backing devolution and proportional representation (coalitions force cooperation), but says Burnham will lose unless he improves public spending efficiency to justify higher taxes.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: A Burnham-led agenda means higher taxes plus devolution; watch spending-efficiency credibility.

insights.claim: Collier views Kemi Badenoch's tax-cutting as a coherent alternative to Burnham's tax-raising, offering voters a genuine choice, but says she must apologize for previous Conservative governments (Boris Johnson, Liz Truss) to win.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: UK next-election framing likely low-tax vs high-tax.

insights.claim: Collier distrusts Nigel Farage's Reform party as over-centralized around one person without in-depth policy knowledge, and sees a whiff of nostalgia in Rupert Lowe's Restore party.
insights.speaker: Paul Collier
insights.so_what: Skeptical view on Reform governing competence, relevant to UK policy risk pricing.
insights.quote: I'm wary of um uh of a of a of this highly centralized uh Farage
